extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and other stakeholders interested in peer review systems and scholarly publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Critically assessing scholarly work about peer review (and manuscripts proposing peer-review innovations), focusing on methodological transparency, evidence support, clarity of claims, and handling of biases and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about study design and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the study design (e.g., narrative review vs systematic review) and acknowledge limitations arising from that choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the comment: 'It appears to be a narrative review, and as such it does not have a standardized, reproducible methodology that you associate with a systematic review. This should be acknowledged as a limitation; as with all narrative reviews there's the concern that references have been selectively chosen...'. Recommend stating strengths and limitations near the beginning of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims with appropriate evidence or label as opinion/prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: All substantive assertions—especially strong evaluative claims about efficiency, superiority, or harms—should be backed by appropriate references; if no empirical evidence exists, label the statement as a prediction or opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the comment: change '...that is more efficient, democratic, and accountable...' to '...that we predict to be more efficient...' when lacking direct evidence. Remove or qualify sentences like 'PRE is much cheaper, legitimate, unbiased, faster, and more efficient alternative...' unless supported by research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define key terms and use precise language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid vague or imprecise terms (e.g., 'oligarchic research institutes') and clarify phrases that could be misleading (e.g., 'evidence-based' vs 'publicly verifiable').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the comment: request to elaborate what is meant by 'oligarchic research institutes' and to reword statements like 'while assessments of articles can never be evidence-based without the publication of referee reports..' to more precise phrasing. Use correct terminology (e.g., 'oligopolistic' vs 'oligarchic' when appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace claims to specific sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting a specific finding, explicitly indicate which referenced study or paper supports that finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Journals with higher transparency ratings, moreover, were less likely to accept flawed papers and showed a higher impact as measured by Google Scholar’s h5-index' — the reviewer asks: 'which previously referenced paper is this finding from?'. Authors should link the claim to the precise citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of evidence and note limitations (modelling vs real-world)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between modelling/preprint evidence and empirical, real-world studies and indicate the strength and limitations of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment example: a cited pre-print modeling study (D’Andrea & O’Dwyer, 2017) should be presented with caveats; authors should seek or note whether 'real world' studies corroborate modeled findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-attributing causality to peer review alone
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing outcomes like research quality failures or retractions, avoid implying that peer review is the sole cause; acknowledge multiple contributing agents (authors, editors, reviewers, institutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the comment: retractions arise from 'multiple failures from multiple players' and statements should reflect multifactorial causation rather than sole blame on peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain roles and responsibilities in proposed peer-review models
rubrics_metrics.description: If proposing new or hybrid peer-review systems, clearly state what roles editors, reviewers, and the community will have (e.g., gatekeeping, inviting reviewers, moderation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer asks whether editors would be 'responsible for finding/inviting reviewers' in future innovations and how editors would be selected (e.g., democratically nominated). Authors should spell out responsibilities and governance mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address reviewer selection bias and workload distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how reviewer choice/selection mechanisms will avoid concentration of reviewing on a minority of papers/reviewers and mitigate incentives for people to review only 'interesting' or high-prestige papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the comment: concern that if reviewers freely choose papers, 'people will end up reviewing a minority of papers in disproportionately high numbers'. Authors should propose mechanisms (assignment, incentives, quotas) to prevent selection bias and uneven workloads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss advantages, disadvantages, and abuse/gaming potential of alternatives (e.g., PRE, peer endorsement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each alternative peer-review model, enumerate potential benefits and drawbacks, and explicitly consider risks of abuse (e.g., author-recommended reviewers leading to higher acceptance rates, fake reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment suggests elaborating on peer review by endorsement and citing studies showing author-recommended reviewers are more likely to recommend acceptance; mention historical cases of fake peer reviews and how proposed systems would prevent such gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide mechanistic detail for process claims (e.g., speed, cost savings)
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming reduced processing time, lower cost, or greater efficiency, explain the specific mechanisms and conditions under which these gains occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer requests elaboration on 'depending on the state of the manuscript, submissions can be published much more rapidly, as relatively little processing is required' — authors should detail what processing is reduced and when that applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone down or qualify broad evaluative language where unsupported
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid absolute adjectives like 'cheaper', 'legitimate', 'unbiased' for entire systems unless broadly evidenced; otherwise present such claims as viewpoints or hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the comment: advise removing or qualifying sweeping statements (e.g., about PRE) when not backed by evidence; use cautious language or provide supporting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support assertions that characterize the literature with citations
rubrics_metrics.description: If claiming that a body of literature 'should be extremely worrisome' or similar, provide citations to the studies that justify this characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer flagged the sentence claiming the corpus of studies 'should be extremely worrisome' and asked for references. Authors should back evaluative characterizations of literatures with representative citations.
